newsitem.title: FRANCE: France seeks 2-year Bosnia force extension.
newsitem.headline: France seeks 2-year Bosnia force extension.

text.p: France wants a NATO-led peace force to stay in Bosnia for two more years, being gradually phased out and passing responsibility to the Bosnian authorities, Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said on Tuesday.

He said when the mandate of the current peace Implementation Force (IFOR) expires at the end of this year, there should be a continued, smaller international military presence during a two-year "stabilisation period" to be approved on Thursday.
He said the aim should be a step-by-step withdrawal of the force to be completed by January 1, 1999.
However Western diplomats said other powers, notably the United States, were unwilling to commit themselves to two years now and were leaning towards a one-year mandate.

Bosnia's three-member collective presidency and foreign ministers of the international Contact Group and other major powers will meet in Paris to approve guiding principles for the civilian aspects of the stabilisation plan, intended to cement the year-old Dayton peace accords.

De Charette said the creating of a post-IFOR force was not on the agenda for Thursday's half-day conference, but he agreed with a questioner that the plan was being adopted on the assumption that there would be a continued military presence.

"It seems reasonable, wise and prudent to have an international military force in the two-year consolidation period. It should gradually transfer responsibility for law and order to local authorities and the police," he told a news conference.
"That means we want a smaller international presence than at present, to be reduced step-by-step towards zero, with a complete withdrawal by January 1, 1999," he said.
De Charette said France and its European Union partners were willing to continue to shoulder the same proportion of responsibility as they had in IFOR.
But in a veiled reference to the United States, he said that if one of the major partners were to withdraw, Paris would do the same.
He was speaking on the eve of a meeting with U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher, at which he acknowledged the issue was likely to be discussed.

Washington has not yet formally committed itself to keeping its troops in Bosnia beyond the end of this year, although Clinton administration officials have been preparing the ground for such a decision since last week's presidential re-election.
